title: Network reader
description: Read real ip, ss, resolv.conf, /etc/hosts, resolvectl, host and ping output from Mira's Debian 13 laptop, and find the address, the gateway, the DNS server and the listening ports.
intro: These commands ran on Mira's laptop on the studio network, and you replay what they printed. After each scene, answer from the output: the right line is highlighted once you pick. The addresses come from ranges reserved for documentation, so they never clash with real networks.
takeaways: `ip addr show` lists each interface with its addresses: `inet` lines are IPv4, `inet6` lines IPv6, and the number after the slash is the prefix length. `lo` is the loopback interface, `127.0.0.1` and `::1`.
`ip route show` lists the IPv4 routes; the `default via` line names the gateway (router) for everything outside the local network. `ip -6 route show` does the same for IPv6.
`ss -tulpn` lists listening TCP and UDP sockets with numeric ports; only root sees the process names of other users' sockets. Port 22 is SSH, 80 HTTP, 53 DNS.

`/etc/hosts` maps names to addresses locally and is checked first; `/etc/resolv.conf` names the DNS server (`nameserver`) and the search domain. With systemd-resolved, it points at the local stub `127.0.0.53`, and `resolvectl status` shows the real DNS servers.

`host name` asks DNS for a name's addresses, and `host address` asks for the name. `ping` tests whether a host answers; `Name or service not known` means the name didn't resolve, before any packet was sent.

For 010-160: `ifconfig`, `route` and `netstat` (package net-tools) are the older tools that `ip addr`, `ip route` and `ss` replace. They live in `/sbin`, which isn't in a normal user's PATH on Debian.

RFC 3849: IPv6 address prefix reserved for documentation

scenes.title: Addresses and routes
scenes.text: Mira looks at her laptop's interfaces and where it sends traffic.

notes.ip-addr: `eth0@if…` is the wired interface. The `fe80::` address is a link-local IPv6 address that every IPv6 interface makes for itself.

questions.prompt: What is the laptop's IPv4 address, with its prefix length?
questions.why: The `inet` line under `eth0` holds it. `127.0.0.1` belongs to the loopback, `192.0.2.255` is the broadcast address (`brd`), and `192.0.2.1` is the gateway.

questions.prompt: Which address is the default gateway for IPv4?
questions.why: `default via` names the router that gets every packet with no more specific route. The other line covers the local network, reached directly.

scenes.title: Who is listening?
scenes.text: Mira checks which programs accept connections on her laptop, first as herself, then with `sudo`.

notes.ss: As a normal user, the Process column stays empty: Mira may not see other users' processes.
notes.ss-sudo: `systemd-resolve` is the local DNS stub; the sockets on `127.0.0.11` belong to Docker's built-in DNS in the capture's container, which a normal laptop doesn't have.

questions.prompt: Which program listens on TCP port 22?
questions.why: Only root sees the process names. The `0.0.0.0:22` line ends in `sshd`.

questions.prompt: On which port does nginx accept web requests?
questions.why: The `0.0.0.0:80` line belongs to nginx. 443 would be HTTPS, which isn't set up on this laptop.

scenes.title: How names are resolved
scenes.text: Mira looks at the two files that decide how her laptop turns names into addresses, and asks systemd-resolved which DNS server it really uses.

notes.resolv-conf: On Debian with systemd-resolved, this file is written by resolved: programs ask the local stub, and the stub asks the real server.

questions.prompt: Which DNS server does the laptop really ask?
questions.why: `/etc/resolv.conf` only names the local stub `127.0.0.53`. `resolvectl status` shows the server behind it.

questions.prompt: Mira types `host build`. Which line makes the short name work?
questions.why: The search domain is appended to names without a dot, so `build` is tried as `build.tuxpixel.example`.

scenes.title: Look up and ping
scenes.text: Mira asks DNS about the build server, then checks that it answers, and tries a server that doesn't exist yet.

notes.ping: The name has an IPv6 address too, and ping used it. `ping -4` forces IPv4.

questions.answer: The name couldn't be resolved, so no packet was sent
distractors: The server is down and didn't answer
questions.why: A host that is down shows lost packets in the statistics. Here ping stopped at the name lookup.

questions.prompt: How many of the three echo requests to the build server got an answer?
questions.why: The statistics line counts sent and received packets: 0% packet loss.

scenes.title: The older tools (010-160)
scenes.text: An old guide tells Mira to use `ifconfig`, `route` and `netstat`. They come from the net-tools package, installed on this laptop for the capture.

notes.ifconfig: `ifconfig` is in `/sbin`, which isn't in a normal user's PATH on Debian. With the full path it works.

questions.prompt: Why did plain `ifconfig` fail for Mira?
questions.answer: Its directory isn't in her PATH
questions.why: The shell searches only the PATH directories. `/sbin/ifconfig` runs fine as Mira.

questions.prompt: In `route -n`, which line is the default gateway?
questions.answer: The one with destination `0.0.0.0` and gateway `192.0.2.1`
distractors: The one with the `U` flag only
questions.why: `route` writes the default route as destination `0.0.0.0` with the `G` (gateway) flag; `ip route` calls it `default via`.
